title: Payment API 503 Service Unavailable During Checkout Surge
logs:
2026-08-10 14:15:02 [ERROR] payment.db.pool: connection acquisition timeout after 5000ms. active=50 idle=0 max=50 queue=284
2026-08-10 14:15:05 [FATAL] payment.checkout: Database connection pool exhausted. Returning 503 to ingress.
root_cause: Database connection pool exhaustion caused by concurrent spike exceeding the default 50 connection ceiling in PgBouncer pooler.
attempted_fixes: Inspected database primary CPU (was 24%, healthy)
Checked read replica replication lag (0ms)
successful_resolution: Increased DB connection pool max_connections from 50 to 100 in ConfigMap and rolled payment pods gracefully.
post_mortem_summary: During the mid-day promotional checkout surge, the Payment API saturated its 50-connection pool while Aurora Postgres had ample CPU capacity. Increasing pool limit to 100 immediately alleviated queue depth.
lessons_learned: Payment API pool limit must match ingress throughput expectations; database connection limits were under-allocated relative to cluster pod counts.
hindsight_memories: INC-0101: Payment API experienced HTTP 503 caused by database connection pool exhaustion on AWS Kubernetes.
INC-0101: Pool saturation symptom showed active=50, idle=0, queue=284 with database CPU remaining healthy under 25%.
INC-0101: Increasing DB connection pool from 50 to 100 successfully resolved the Payment API 503 outage.
INC-0101: Aurora PostgreSQL CPU was not the bottleneck; PgBouncer client pool size was the constraint.

title: Payment API HTTP 503 and Connection Timeouts Following Nightly Deployment
symptoms: Payment worker pods crashing with CrashLoopBackOff
logs:
2026-09-02 03:40:12 [ERROR] payment.db: failed to connect to aurora-primary.internal:5432: password authentication failed for user 'payment_app'
2026-09-02 03:40:15 [FATAL] payment.main: Database connection timeout. Pod terminating.
root_cause: Automated AWS Secrets Manager credential rotation failure during CI/CD rollout; new pods booted with stale cached password while DB had rotated secret.
attempted_fixes: Attempted increasing connection pool from 100 to 150 (FAILED: blind repetition of INC-0101 fix did not resolve authentication failure)
successful_resolution: Force-refreshed Kubernetes Secret from AWS Secrets Manager using ExternalSecrets operator sync and rotated payment service credentials.
failed_fixes: Increasing connection pool size failed: connection pool was empty because authentication failed before any connection could be established.
pattern_type: Pattern B: 503 -> Credential Rotation Failure (Same Symptom != Same Root Cause)
post_mortem_summary: Identical HTTP 503 symptoms to INC-0101 occurred, but investigating logs revealed password auth failure rather than pool saturation. Blindly increasing pool failed. Secret synchronization resolved the issue.
lessons_learned: Do not assume 503 on Payment API is always pool exhaustion; verify whether handshake fails at auth vs socket queue. Credential rotation pipelines need automated pre-flight validation.
hindsight_memories: INC-0145: Payment API experienced HTTP 503 with database connection timeout following deployment v2.6.
INC-0145: Increasing connection pool FAILED because root cause was database credential rotation mismatch, not pool exhaustion.
INC-0145: Successful resolution was refreshing AWS Secrets Manager synced credentials via ExternalSecrets operator.
INC-0145: CRITICAL LESSON: HTTP 503 on Payment API can be caused by either pool exhaustion OR auth failure; check auth logs before touching pool size.

title: Authentication Service High CPU & OOMKilled Pod Termination
symptoms: Memory usage ramp from 500MB to 4096MB limit

2026-08-14 09:30:10 [WARN] auth.session: session cache entries: 1,840,291. Heap threshold exceeded.
2026-08-14 09:30:12 [FATAL] kernel: oom-killer: killed process auth-service (pid 41) total-vm:4194304kB
root_cause: Unbounded in-memory session token cache with missing TTL expiration, causing heap memory leak under high concurrent user logins.
attempted_fixes: Restarted ECS tasks (temporarily restored service for 4 hours, then memory ramped back to 4GB OOMKilled)
successful_resolution: Patched session cache in auth-service v4.1 with sliding 15-minute TTL eviction policy and offloaded token storage to Redis.
failed_fixes: Restarting tasks was only a temporary mitigation; failed to prevent recurrence without code patch.
pattern_type: Pattern C: High CPU -> Memory Leak -> Restart Temporary -> Code Patch Permanent
post_mortem_summary: Session cache leaked memory linearly with active user logins. Restarting containers bought 4 hours of buffer, but permanent stability required LRU eviction and external Redis session store.
lessons_learned: In-memory caches must always specify hard maximum entry bounds and strict TTL policies. Service restarts are mitigating workarounds, not root cause fixes.
hindsight_memories: INC-0210: Authentication Service experienced OOMKilled (exit code 137) caused by unbounded in-memory session cache leak.
INC-0210: Restarting ECS containers only bought 4 hours of stability before memory re-exhausted.
INC-0210: Permanent resolution was patching auth-service with Redis-backed session store and 15-min LRU eviction.
INC-0210: Beware of relying on container restarts for memory leaks; permanent fix requires code/cache bounds.

title: Order Service High Latency & Cascading Thread Starvation
symptoms: Tomcat thread pool exhaustion (200/200 threads busy)

2026-08-22 16:20:06 [ERROR] org.apache.tomcat.util.threads: All 200 worker threads busy. Requests queuing up.
root_cause: Third-party shipping carrier API degraded, taking 9.8s per request. Order Service had synchronous 10s timeout with no circuit breaker, saturating all worker threads.

successful_resolution: Implemented Resilience4j Circuit Breaker with 1.5s timeout, fast-fallback stub, and asynchronous background webhook sync.
failed_fixes: Increasing thread pool size failed because slow synchronous downstream calls will inevitably consume all available threads.
pattern_type: Pattern D: High Latency -> Third-Party Dependency -> Circuit Breaker Tuning
post_mortem_summary: Downstream carrier partner outage caused upstream thread exhaustion across all Order Service pods. Doubling threads worsened latency. Circuit breaker with fast fallback restored order checkout within 2 minutes.
lessons_learned: Never make synchronous calls to third-party external APIs in the critical checkout path without circuit breakers and aggressive timeouts.
hindsight_memories: INC-0240: Order Service P99 latency degraded to 8.5s due to third-party shipping carrier API slowdown.
INC-0240: Doubling thread pool from 200 to 400 failed and caused deeper memory pressure.
INC-0240: Successful resolution was Resilience4j circuit breaker with 1.5s timeout and asynchronous fallback queue.
INC-0240: Do not increase thread pools for downstream latency issues; enforce circuit breaking.

title: Order Service Out of Direct Memory In Netty ByteBuf Allocator
logs:

2026-09-15 21:30:06 [FATAL] order.dispatch: JVM direct memory exhausted (used: 2048MB, max: 2048MB). Exiting process.
root_cause: WebClient reactive HTTP filter failed to release unpooled ByteBuf buffers on aborted client connections during high traffic.
attempted_fixes: Increased JVM heap (-Xmx4g to -Xmx8g) (FAILED: direct off-heap memory is governed by -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize, not heap size)

failed_fixes: Increasing -Xmx heap size failed because Netty buffers allocate off-heap in direct memory.
post_mortem_summary: Classic Netty off-heap leak occurred when mobile clients disconnected mid-request. Increasing Java heap did nothing. Releasing reference counts fixed the leak permanently.
lessons_learned: Do not confuse Java Heap OOM with Direct Memory OOM. Verify Netty buffer leak detector with -Dio.netty.leakDetection.level=ADVANCED.
hindsight_memories: INC-0375: Order Service crashed with Direct buffer memory OOM caused by Netty ByteBuf leak on aborted client connections.
INC-0375: Increasing JVM heap -Xmx failed because leak was off-heap direct memory.
INC-0375: Fix was adding ReferenceCountUtil.release in WebClient error handler and setting -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=4g.

title: Inventory Service Deadlock on Concurrent Warehouse Stock Decrement

post_mortem_summary: Asymmetric lock acquisition order across bulk checkout transactions caused deadlocks. Enforcing deterministic ascending lock order eliminated deadlocks completely.
lessons_learned: Any transaction locking multiple rows must sort row identifiers deterministically before issuing SELECT FOR UPDATE.
hindsight_memories: INC-0420: Inventory Service experienced PostgreSQL deadlocks (40P01) during multi-item checkouts.
INC-0420: Increasing deadlock_timeout failed and worsened latency.
INC-0420: Successful resolution was sorting row lock acquisitions deterministically by sku_id ASC in transaction code.

hindsight_memories: INC-0540: Order Service Kafka consumer group suffered rebalance storm due to slow billing transaction exceeding max.poll.interval.ms (300s).
